name: Ferrocaine
description: Ferrocaine is a crude but effective street synthesis of a dissociative analgesic compound, believed to be derived from a degraded ketamine analogue base cut with a synthetic opioid receptor partial agonist. It's cooked in Shelf labs from sourced industrial precursors and sold in small crystalline capsules stamped with a crude iron cross. It works — it suppresses pain effectively — but the synthesis is inconsistent and every batch is slightly different. Shelf medics know it well because they see what it does when a batch goes wrong.
effects: Mild dissociation that reduces psychological distress from injury
Functional combat capacity maintained through moderate wounds
Slight euphoric edge that sustains morale under pressure
side_effects: Batch inconsistency means dosing is unreliable — what worked last time may not work this time
Dissociation can deepen into incapacitation with stronger batches
Significant addiction risk due to opioid receptor activity
Hepatotoxicity with regular use due to industrial precursor impurities
Respiratory depression risk with high doses or when combined with alcohol
Withdrawal syndrome including severe pain hypersensitivity — chronic users become physically dependent
cultural_context: Ferrocaine is what you take when you can't afford Nullocaine and you need to keep moving. It's a Shelf fixture — every gang has a supply, every runner knows where to get it, and every Shelf medic has protocols for treating Ferrocaine OD. The iron cross stamp has become a symbol in Shelf art and tattoo culture, representing endurance and suffering accepted. The chemists who produce reliable FC are respected figures; the ones who cook inconsistent batches are blamed for deaths and sometimes violently held accountable. There's a quiet tragedy in Ferrocaine dependency — people who got hooked because they needed it to survive are now sick from the thing that kept them alive.
story_hooks: A batch of FC has hit the Shelf that produces reliable, clean pain suppression with no dissociation — better than pharmaceutical Nullocaine, at Φ20 a capsule. Someone with real chemistry knowledge is cooking it, and the major suppliers want to know who before they cut into their market.

A runner with a Ferrocaine dependency realizes their tolerance has climbed so high that therapeutic doses no longer cover combat pain — they need to either escalate to dangerous levels or find a way to detox during an active job.

The Shelf chemist behind the FC stamp has been arrested by Lazarus corporate security — not for making illegal drugs, but because the synthesis process they developed accidentally mirrors a patented Lazarus precursor reaction, and the corp wants the formula.
